text.p: At the age of 12, a boy from Cuba wrote to President Franklin Roosevelt asking him to write back and enclose $10 "green American."
"If you like give me a ten dollar bill green American in the letter. I have not seen a ten dollar bill green American and I would like to have one of them," the young Fidel Castro wrote.

There is no recorded response to the letter from Cuba's future revolutionary leader, and no way to know whether a letter or a $10 bill from the U.S. president might have changed the course of history. But the request, written by hand on Nov. 6, 1940, is now on display at the National Archives.

The archives bulge with billions of rarely seen original documents ranging from Napoleon's wedding announcement to President Richard Nixon's resignation speech. Now the curators have mounted a sampling of "American Originals," the second year-long show of its kind, designed to give the public a taste of the archives' richness and a glimpse of the nation's history.
The exhibit is a quiet one -- no special effects, no videos, no interactive modules, simply the power of these yellowing papers from the past.
"Documents can be compelling for different reasons," curator Stacey Bredhoff said. "It's not hard to capture the public's imagination with the materials we have here."
NIXON LETTER: NATIONAL TRAUMA IN A SENTENCE
Nixon's resignation letter, she said, "represents this major national trauma, rolling all of that up somehow into a one-sentence document."

A seven-year ledger in which Gen. George Washington kept his meticulous Continental Army expense account, entering payments for everything from spies to blacksmiths, "shows us something human about this mythological father of our country who was larger than life," she said.

And a report signed by Robert E. Lee, then commander of the army unit that squelched John Brown's anti-slavery revolt at Harper's Ferry, West Virginia, "represents a milestone event in our history," she said. Lee later commanded the South's forces in the U.S. Civil War.

Not all the documents belonged to men of might and power. Included is a letter from suffragette Susan B. Anthony demanding that women get the vote; a treaty granting territory in the Black Hills to the Sioux Indians, which whites reneged on when they decided there might be gold there, and the arrest records of Rosa Park, a black woman whose refusal to surrender her bus seat to a white person helped launch the U.S. civil rights movement.

Some of the documents in the exhibit are well-known. Tourists come in asking to see John Kennedy's 1961 inaugural address or the Louisiana Purchase Treaty, encased in purple velvet and gold brocade and formalising France's sale of 828,000 square miles (2 million sq km) west of the Mississippi for a paltry $15 million.
But some are obscure -- like young Castro's letter or the expedition shopping list of explorers Lewis and Clark. And still others are quiet reminders of monumental moments.

When his men set forth for the D-Day invasion of Nazi-held France, Gen. Dwight Eisenhower scribbled a note and slipped it into his pocket, accepting total responsibility in case of failure. "He wanted it to be clear that the decision to attack at this time and place was his, and his alone," Bredhoff said. "And he was prepared for the fact that it might fail."

D-Day did not fail. But a reminder of what failure could have meant is also found in the exhibit -- handwritten notes by Heinrich Himmler, chief of the Nazi SS Guard and architect of the "final solution" for the Jews. Those notes ended up in U.S. hands as part of the Nuremberg war crime trials.
